{{Short description|Mathematical technique for vector bundles}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''splitting principle''' is a technique used to reduce questions about [[vector bundle]]s to the case of [[line bundle]]s. In the theory of vector bundles, one often wishes to simplify computations, for example of [[Chern classes]]. Often computations are well understood for line bundles and for direct sums of line bundles. Then the splitting principle can be quite useful.

==Statement==
One version of the splitting principle is captured in the following theorem. This theorem holds for complex vector bundles and cohomology with [[integer]] coefficients. It also holds for real vector bundles and cohomology with <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> coefficients.

{{math_theorem|Let <math>\xi\colon E\rightarrow X</math> be a vector bundle of rank <math>n</math> over a [[paracompact space]] <math>X</math>.  There exists a space <math>Y=Fl(E)</math>, called the flag bundle associated to <math>E</math>, and a map <math>p\colon Y\rightarrow X</math> such that

#the induced cohomology homomorphism <math>p^*\colon H^*(X)\rightarrow H^*(Y)</math> is injective, and
#the pullback bundle <math>p^*\xi\colon p^*E\rightarrow Y</math> breaks up as a direct sum of line bundles: <math>p^*(E)=L_1\oplus L_2\oplus\cdots\oplus L_n.</math>}}

In the complex case, the line bundles <math>L_i</math> or their first [[characteristic class]]es are called '''Chern roots.'''

Another version of the splitting principle concerns real vector bundles and their [[Complexification|complexifications]]:<ref>H. Blane Lawson and Marie-Louise Michelsohn, ''Spin Geometry'', Proposition 11.2.</ref>

{{math_theorem|Let <math>\xi\colon E\rightarrow X</math> be a real vector bundle of rank <math>2n</math> over a paracompact space <math>X</math>. There exists a space <math>Y</math> and a map <math>p\colon Y\rightarrow X</math> such that

#the induced cohomology homomorphism <math>p^*\colon H^*(X)\rightarrow H^*(Y)</math> is injective, and
#the pullback bundle <math>p^*\xi\colon p^*E\rightarrow Y</math> breaks up as a direct sum of line bundles and their conjugates: <math>p^*(E\otimes \mathbb{C})=L_1\oplus \overline{L_1}\oplus \cdots\oplus L_n\oplus \overline{L_n}.</math>}}

==Consequences==
The fact that <math>p^*\colon H^*(X)\rightarrow H^*(Y)</math> is injective means that any equation which holds in <math>H^*(Y)</math> &mdash; for example, among various Chern classes &mdash; also holds in <math>H^*(X)</math>. Often these equations are easier to understand for direct sums of line bundles than for arbitrary vector bundles. So equations should be understood in <math>Y</math> and then pushed forward to <math>X</math>.

Since vector bundles on <math>X</math> are used to define the [[K-theory]] group <math>K(X)</math>, <math>p^*\colon K(X)\rightarrow K(Y)</math> is also injective for the map <math>p</math> in the first theorem above.<ref>Oscar Randal-Williams, Characteristic classes and K-theory, Corollary 4.3.4, https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~or257/teaching/notes/Kthy.pdf</ref>

Under the splitting principle, characteristic classes for complex vector bundles correspond to [[symmetric polynomials]] in the first Chern classes of [[complex line]] bundles; these are the [[Chern class]]es.
